Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From first endpoint to global fleet: 14 more debuts for managed endpoints and HyperPod Inference.
  • In September, Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date releases in review covered 13 launches that shortened the path from a model to a production endpoint.
  • It has been revealed that once a model is in production, the questions change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From first endpoint to global fleet: 14 more debuts for managed endpoints and HyperPod Inference.

In September, Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date releases in review covered 13 launches that shortened the path from a model to a production endpoint. Most of them answered one question: how do I get this model serving quickly and reliably? This post covers the 14 launches that came next, bringing the total for 2026 to 27.

It has been revealed that once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them.

For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway and the Global Inference Gateway deliver the routing and multi-Region work, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts.

To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the introduces from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat.

Figure 1: The five stages in this post and the introduces in each.

The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console.

Inference recommendations debuted in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A newly introduced agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents.

Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI.

The April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs, then Inference optimization. Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model.

In a recent development, sageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio.

Blog: LLM optimization integration for Amazon SageMaker Python SDK.

Benchmarking and recommendations previously required SageMaker AI Studio or direct Boto3 calls. They are now part of the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (version 3.17.0 and later), the same interface teams use for training and deployment, so the workflow fits into notebooks, CI pipelines, and MLOps workflows. You can benchmark a live endpoint against your workload traffic, generate ranked recommendations for a latency, throughput, or cost goal, and deploy the top-ranked configuration to a real-time endpoint in a single call.

Recent findings suggest that the SDK also supports longer workflows. You can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM, and you can resume from a completed job so that deployment happens in a different notebook or pipeline stage without re-running the benchmarks.

Developer guide: Get recommendations for models with LoRA adapters.

Many teams use LoRA adapters to specialize one foundation model for several use cases. Each adapter kept in GPU memory reduces the number of concurrent requests the endpoint can serve, and the right balance depends on the instance type, the number of adapters, and the traffic profile.

Inference recommendations now accept adapters as Model Package Amazon Resource Names (ARNs), for adapters produced by SageMaker fine-tuning, or as S3 URIs, for adapters from external pipelines such as Hugging Face PEFT. SageMaker AI benchmarks combinations of adapter count and concurrency on real GPU infrastructure and returns ranked results for your workload. The output lists both formats for every adapter. The recommended deployment uses SageMaker Inference Components, with one component for the base model and one for each adapter, so you can add, update, or remove an adapter without disrupting the base model or the other adapters.

Blog: Right-size generative AI endpoints with concurrency sweeps on Amazon SageMaker AI.

Right-sizing an endpoint means finding the highest concurrency it can sustain without breaching latency or error targets. Until now, that meant picking concurrency levels by hand, running a sweep, checking the results against the service level agreement (SLA), and repeating with a narrower range whenever the model or instance changed.

It has been revealed that inference recommendations now include a search that finds that boundary directly. Set search_recipe to max-concurrency-under-sla and supply targets for any combination of maximum TTFT, maximum time per output token, maximum end-to-end latency, and maximum error rate. The benchmarking engine (AIPerf) starts from a broad range, narrows it based on which probes pass or fail, and converges in fewer iterations than a linear sweep. The result reports the largest passing concurrency (feasible_max) or, if no level qualifies, the smallest failing one (infeasible_min).

According to recent reports, the search uses the same CreateAIWorkloadConfig and CreateAIBenchmarkJob APIs as concurrency sweeps. Optional parameters (concurrency_min, concurrency_max, search_max_iterations, and search_initial_points) bound the cost and speed up convergence.

Blog: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent.

It has been revealed that engineers increasingly ask their coding agent which instance and container to use. Without grounded knowledge and access to real benchmarks, the agent can only guess, and a wrong instance choice shows up later as missed latency targets or wasted spend.

The aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. Engineers describe what they need in plain language, and the agent can do the following:.

In a recent development, answers are grounded in measured performance and delivered as SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that engineers review and run under their own credentials. Setup takes about 10 minutes. The skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces.

For the support team, one recommendation job that includes all four adapters, followed by a concurrency search against the 500 millisecond TTFT target, replaces the manual sweeps they ran in April. The engineer who owns it can start the job from a notebook or ask a coding agent to run it.

The support assistant does not run alone. An embedding model, a reranker, and a small classifier that routes tickets live in the same account, and each uses a fraction of a GPU. On a standard endpoint, each model copy still held a whole accelerator, so the team ran out of placement slots while GPU memory sat unused.

Developer guide: Inference Components in the SageMaker AI Console.

Sources indicate that with Inference Components, you can host several models on one endpoint and size and scale each model separately. Until now, they were available only through the SDK and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Every create, resize, and scaling policy had to be scripted, and there was no single view of what each model was using.

In the SageMaker AI console, you can now create, view, enhancement, and delete inference components:.

The console calls the same SageMaker AI APIs as the SDK and CLI, so teams can start on the console and automate later, or manage scripted components visually.

Blog: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints.

GPU partitioning uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology to divide one physical GPU into as many as seven partitions, depending on the accelerator. Each partition has dedicated GPU compute and memory, with complete hardware isolation. You define the partition layout when you create an endpoint for inference components and choose a partition type for each component. Applications keep invoking models by inference component name, so client code does not change.

MIG isolates GPU compute and memory between partitions. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, host memory, networking, storage, and endpoint routing. You pay the standard rate for the full instance-hour, so the saving comes from placing more models on each instance, not from a lower hourly price.

Figure 2: Three small models on three GPUs, compared with the same models in partitions of one GPU.

For the support team, the embedding model, the reranker, and the classifier now run in separate partitions of one GPU on a single endpoint, and the team manages every component, including the assistant and its adapters, from the console.

Industry observers note that the team’s next model is a reasoning model whose weights alone exceed the GPU memory of any single instance. They have also noticed that long, retrieval-heavy prompts slow token generation for every other user on the endpoint. For a model this size, they move the workload to HyperPod Inference, which gives them dedicated clusters and Kubernetes-native control. The support assistant stays on managed endpoints.

Blog: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference.

It has been revealed that part 1 covered two building blocks for large models on HyperPod: disaggregated prefill and decode in Inference Operator v3.2, and KV-aware routing as part of the managed tiered KV cache. This launch adds multi-node serving and changes who operates the stack. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source inference framework that provides multi-node sharded serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. Teams could already run Dynamo on their own Kubernetes clusters, but they had to build and operate everything around it: placing all the nodes of a replica together, wiring Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking so prefill can hand its KV cache to decode at hardware speed, maintaining serving images, and recovering when one failed node takes down a multi-node replica.

According to recent reports, with this launch, Dynamo runs as a managed serving engine on HyperPod. Dynamo makes the serving decisions: how the model is sharded, how prefill and decode are split, and where each request goes. HyperPod provides what those decisions depend on:.

The capabilities Dynamo brings to HyperPod are:.

There are three ways to start. Teams running Dynamo on self-managed Kubernetes can bring their existing DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) manifests largely unchanged. Teams already on HyperPod Inference can upgrade the add-on and add a short dynamoSpec block to an existing InferenceEndpointConfig, which HyperPod converts into a DGD, while existing endpoints keep serving. Teams new to both can create a cluster with the add-on and Dynamo enabled from the console. In each case, clients call a standard OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so client code does not change.

Managed Dynamo supports vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, and is available in the Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Figure 3: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference.

For the support team, the reasoning model runs as one sharded replica across several nodes, with separate prefill and decode pools. When a node fails, HyperPod replaces it and reschedules the replica without a page to the on-call engineer.

The support assistant now serves customers in North America and Europe, so the team runs endpoints and HyperPod clusters in two Regions. During the US morning peak, requests queue in the US Region while GPUs the team already pays for sit idle in Europe. Some European traffic must also stay in Europe.

According to recent reports, routing decides whether capacity a team owns does useful work. It happens at four levels, and the introduces below cover one level each: which instance serves a request inside an endpoint, which pod inside a HyperPod cluster, which cluster across a fleet, and which Regional endpoint across Regions and accounts.

Figure 4: Routing across Regions and inside each endpoint or cluster, on both deployment paths.

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing.

Applications with long prompts or multi-turn conversations repeat a large prefix across requests. A model server can reuse the matching KV cache, but only if the next request reaches the instance that holds it. Prefix-aware routing, covered in part 1, fingerprints the start of each prompt and sends matching prompts to the same instance. Because it works from request history, its view of each instance’s cache becomes less accurate as the model server adds and evicts entries.

According to recent reports, KV-cache-aware routing uses the cache state the model container reports. The container publishes cache creation and eviction events to a central cache index, and SageMaker AI routes each request to an eligible instance that holds the longest matching cached prefix. This raises cache reuse for long-context prompts, multi-turn conversations, and workloads that share dynamic prompt prefixes.

It works with single-model endpoints and endpoints that use inference components, including LoRA adapters. It supports InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, and the OpenAI-compatible API for Completions and Chat Completions payloads. You turn it on in the endpoint configuration. The first release requires an AWS-verified model container that implements the cache-event, tokenization, metrics, and OpenAI-compatible interfaces. You can track KV cache hit rate in detailed inference observability.

It has been revealed that which one to use. Prefix-aware routing works with any container and needs no container changes. KV-cache-aware routing needs a verified container and tracks the actual cache, which helps most when prefixes vary or caches turn over rapidly.

Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway.

Inside a HyperPod cluster, capacity and demand rarely line up. One pod can be partway through a long-context request with its KV cache nearly full, while the next pod sits idle or already holds the prompt prefix or LoRA adapter the next request needs. Without visibility into that GPU state, upcoming requests queue behind busy pods, and teams add GPUs to protect latency instead of using the ones they have. Each model also had its own endpoint, so clients had to track one endpoint per model.

According to recent reports, the Inference Gateway is a GPU-aware router that installs with the HyperPod Inference Operator add-on and gives each cluster one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for all of its models. For each request, it reads live signals from every model pod and picks the best one, with weights you can tune per workload:.

Compared with round-robin routing, it reduced P99 TTFT by up to 97% on mixed GPU generations and by up to 98% under bursty traffic. It is available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway.

Industry observers note that the Inference Gateway routes within a cluster, and each cluster can serve only the requests sent to it. A request can wait on a saturated cluster in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another. Clients had to choose a cluster themselves, and when a cluster failed, an engineer had to move traffic by hand.

Recent findings suggest that the Global Inference Gateway gives teams one SageMaker-managed endpoint across every cluster they register. For each request, it scores clusters on queue depth, free KV cache, proximity to the caller, and recent error rate, and sends the request to the best one over the AWS private backbone. The Inference Gateway in that cluster still picks the pod. Requests authenticate with SigV4 and IAM. When a cluster becomes saturated or unhealthy, traffic shifts to the next-best cluster in under 30 seconds with no action from the client, and the cluster rejoins the pool when it recovers. Routing weights are tunable, with defaults if you leave them unset.

Adding or removing a model or cluster does not change anything for the applications that call the endpoint. No cluster is reachable until you publish it, and the published resources stay in your account. The Global Inference Gateway is available in the Regions listed in the AWS documentation.

Blog: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.

Recent findings suggest that on managed endpoints, the same idea takes the form of the Cross-Region Inference Routing, managed routing that sends real-time and asynchronous requests across Regional endpoints a team has already deployed, in the same account or in different accounts. You group endpoints that serve the same model under a routing target, and the application invokes the target instead of a specific Regional endpoint. The router does not add capacity, replicate models, or deploy endpoints, and the existing invocation path keeps working.

The router replaces the failover logic teams build themselves today:.

Figure 5: Cross-Region Inference Router request flow.

Sources indicate that the two cross-Region introduces apply the same idea on each deployment path. The team keeps ownership of its clusters and endpoints, and SageMaker supplies the routing, the private connectivity, and the failover.

For the support team, the US morning peak now overflows to capacity in Europe on both paths, and requests that must stay in Europe are restricted to European Regions in the router policy.

Two months after the move, the team adds retrieval to the support assistant, and the average prompt length roughly doubles. TTFT is now higher than it was at launch, but nothing has failed, so every alarm stays green. When the team finds a better configuration, they will need to roll it out on large GPU instances that are hard to get more of.

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints.

Amazon SageMaker AI now continuously monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. When a finding clears its confidence threshold, a notification appears on the AWS Management Console, and the same message arrives by email for teams that work in notebooks and the CLI. The recommended action opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker AI Studio with the finding already filled in, so the analysis, the comparison, and the deployment change happen in one conversation. Nothing deploys until you apply it, and you can turn monitoring off at any time.

There are three types of findings:.

A standard rolling enhancement replaces an endpoint one batch at a time, and every batch runs on newly provisioned instances. On a large GPU fleet, that means finding newly introduced capacity at every step, and an update can fail partway through when the next batch of instances is not available. Each released instance must also finish cleanup before it can be used again, which slows the rollout.

In a recent development, sageMaker AI now updates models in place. It provisions one small batch of additional instances at the start, shifts traffic to that batch, and then updates the instances it frees, reusing them to roll the change across the rest of the fleet. The upgrade still rolls out in stages, but it needs latest capacity only once. For a fleet of 20 instances with a batch size of 2, the update acquires 2 new instances instead of 20. Customers do not need to change anything. As with container caching in part 1, the improvement applies automatically to rolling model updates.

In a recent development, figure 6: A rolling update acquires new instances at every step. An in-place rolling update acquires one batch at the start and reuses the rest of the fleet.

It has been revealed that for the support team, a Drift Watch finding quantifies the TTFT regression and opens a new recommendation job against recent traffic. They roll out the updated model with one batch of extra instances, instead of finding new GPU capacity for every instance in the fleet.

The numbering continues from the 13 rolls out in part 1.

Sources indicate that 14. Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026). A guided, low-code workflow for ranked, benchmarked configurations, with deployment from Studio.

It has been revealed that 15. Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026). Benchmark, recommend, and deploy from a notebook or pipeline, with parallel and resumable jobs.

16. LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026). Benchmarks adapter count against concurrency and deploys adapters as inference components.

In a recent development, 17. SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026). Finds the highest concurrency that meets TTFT, latency, and error-rate targets.

In a recent development, 18. Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026). Instance selection, benchmarking, and run comparison from MCP-compatible coding agents.

19. Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026). Create, scale, and monitor each model on a multi-model endpoint without scripts.

Industry observers note that 20. GPU partitioning with NVIDIA MIG (October 2026). Up to seven isolated partitions per GPU, assigned per inference component.

21. Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026). Multi-node and disaggregated serving, with HyperPod operating the platform underneath.

22. KV-cache-aware routing (November 2026). Routes each request to the instance that holds the longest cached prefix, based on cache events from the container.

23. Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026). One endpoint per cluster with GPU-aware routing, and up to 97% lower P99 TTFT than round-robin.

It has been revealed that 24. Global Inference Gateway for HyperPod (November 2026). One endpoint across clusters and Regions, with failover in under 2 minutes.

25. Cross-Region Inference Router. Routes across Regional and cross-account endpoints over PrivateLink, with overflow and residency guardrails.

It has been revealed that 26. Continuous performance monitoring. Detects latency drift, configuration gaps, and idle capacity, with a guided fix in SageMaker AI Studio.

27. In-place rolling model updates (November 2026). Rolls out model updates with one batch of additional instances at the start, then reuses existing instances across the fleet.

Recent findings suggest that by the end of the year, the support team serves four product lines from one base model, runs its small models on shared GPUs, serves a reasoning model that no single instance can hold, and routes traffic across two Regions with residency controls. It did not need to build its own benchmarking harness, failover logic, or drift monitoring to get there.

Part 1 argued that advantage in AI inference comes from operating an efficient inference stack. These 14 launches apply that argument to the months after launch day. The AWS Experience-Based Acceleration program can help your team put them to work by benchmarking your workloads and configuring your inference stack against your SLAs and cost targets.

On managed endpoints, we blueprint to extend in-place rolling updates in early 2027 with scale-in-first updates, which remove the need for any additional instances during a model revision.

Documentation and getting-started guides for every capability in this post are in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Start with the section that matches your current problem. If your traffic has changed since you deployed, re-run inference recommendations. If you are short on placement slots, move small models onto partitioned GPUs. If requests queue while capacity you own sits idle, register your clusters and endpoints for cross-Region routing.

How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (292 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.

#10826. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1398 w)

Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • Industry observers note that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

Industry observers note that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It states nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

Industry observers note that we wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

Industry observers note that the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

According to recent reports, here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

Recent findings suggest that this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

Recent findings suggest that we compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

It has been revealed that distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

Industry observers note that no single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It highlights how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Industry observers note that gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

In a recent development, catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Sources indicate that feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

Sources indicate that up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

It has been revealed that more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can blueprint around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

It has been revealed that what does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework for Brainprint Authentication

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (201 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.31801v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.

Learning Compact State Abstractions for LLM Agents

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (162 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31800v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.

Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency.
  • Recent findings suggest that this post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS.
  • The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks.

Recent findings suggest that this post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer.

The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything:.

These flows, from estimating benefits to setup, require the following:.

In a recent development, we gave the agent this prompt: “My vLLM fleet serves a legal assistant with 64K-token contexts on p5 instances. Returning conversations take 13 seconds for the first token because the GPU recomputes the full conversation history every turn. How do I fix this?”.

It has been revealed that the agent matches the request to the skill and, in Kiro, asks for approval before loading it. The answer identifies that the latency was caused by cold prefill, and three things in the answer matter for a real deployment. First, it checks for fixes that need no fresh infrastructure. If you turned off prefix caching, turning it back on can speed up back-to-back turns. If the GPU prefix cache hit rate is already above 90% with session affinity, you might not need a shared KV cache. Second, it identifies constraints specific to the legal AI assistant. A shared KV cache can let one tenant tell from response times whether another tenant sent the same text. Cases that must stay isolated get separate caches, and tenants that share a cache add their own ID to the KV hash. Third, it doesn’t guess the size. It asks for the model and TP size, KV data type, replica count and routing, and how long people wait between turns.

Figure 1: The diagnosis and proposed architecture for the legal assistant.

Recent findings suggest that to size the savings, we gave the agent an example fleet of 8 p5 instances that serve 64,000-token prompts for a multi-turn retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant. The agent looked up the GPU and cache node prices and derived the prefill rate and KV size from benchmarks. Finally, the agent recommended two cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes for distributed KV caching. The following figure shows the agent’s summary and the inputs it used.

Industry observers note that figure 2: The agent’s summary and inputs. It looked up both prices in the AWS price list and explains how it arrived at the recompute figure.

We didn’t provide a cache hit rate, which is the share of recomputed tokens the cache would serve. The agent therefore presents scenarios and recommends a KVTrace run to identify the cache hit rate. KVTrace records the KV cache events from vLLM or SGLang. It then replays them offline against a shared KV cache of each candidate size. The recorder never writes token IDs or prompt text. Traces hold block hashes and token counts. Block hashes come from token content, so pass --anonymize-key-file when your prompts are sensitive. The skill records on every GPU server for a representative window, such as a full business day. The agent also notes that freed GPU time turns into dollars only if you run fewer servers or serve more traffic on the same ones.

According to recent reports, figure 3: The top of a KVTrace report from synthetic demo traffic. It recommends the smallest capacity that reaches 90% of the savings ceiling.

We prompted the agent with: “Set up a shared L2 KV cache for LLM inference, starting from scratch.” Before it creates anything, the agent requests your confirmation to set up the suggested cache node count in your Availability Zone, at the estimated price. Once confirmed, it creates the right security group with EFA permissions, and a Valkey 9.1 cluster that uses a custom parameter group with caching eviction policies. LMCache gets its own cache user, with the password in AWS Secrets Manager. The agent prepares the GPU servers and starts one LMCache server per GPU server. Then it checks the cluster with a small test object and confirms that repeated prompts load their KV state from the cache over Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA). On a GPU fleet, the skill checks the measured L2 share against the KVTrace prediction. For the full setup with every command, see Getting started with distributed KV caching in the Amazon ElastiCache documentation.

In a recent development, prompt: “My LMCache server connects to the ElastiCache cluster and BLOB.RDMA_HELLO succeeds, but actual data transfers are failing. INFO largeobj shows rdma_write_errors climbing. What’s wrong?”.

Following the skill’s troubleshooting guide, the agent reasons from the symptom pattern and identifies the likely cause as a security group that blocks EFA traffic between its own members. It provides you commands to check and fix the rule.

Figure 4: The agent explains the symptom, then gives commands to check and fix the security group.

You can get the distributed KV caching skill or the AWS MCP Server from the Agent Toolkit for AWS. Then describe your problem or ask your AI agent to cut costs and latency on your GPU fleet to get started. To learn more about distributed KV caching with ElastiCache and the performance benchmarks see the AWS blog. You can see getting started with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) at Amazon ElastiCache documentation and learn more about KVTrace at the GitHub repo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
  • Sources indicate that we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

Sources indicate that we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

According to recent reports, daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

In a recent development, we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

In a recent development, radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

According to recent reports, 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Sources indicate that every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

Recent findings suggest that the service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Industry observers note that cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

According to recent reports, we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.

Sources indicate that advancements in model post-training are interesting because they can improve how efficiently models handle specialized tasks and complex instructions. For businesses building AI-powered applications, selecting the right model is also an important cost consideration. A larger model is not always necessary for every task, and using appropriately sized models can help balance performance, latency, and API expenses. I've been exploring how model selection and resource optimization influence the overall cost of AI agent systems. This guide shares practical approaches to optimizing AI agent costs: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-agent-cost-optimization.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (242 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.31789v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and transfer across turbine scales. Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers $St=fD/U_\infty$ of 0.2-0.6 (where $f$, $D$, and $U_\infty$ are the motion frequency, rotor diameter, and inflow velocity) for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW ($D=126$ m) and International Energy Agency 22 MW ($D=284$ m) turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator framework combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes. Trained on the 5 MW fixed and $St=0.2$-$0.5$ cases, the framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through $St=0.6$ (mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of $D$), while 10% planar sampling preserves near-dense accuracy (relative $L_2$ error 0.0689 versus 0.0684). Applying transfer learning from the 5 MW to the 22 MW turbine lowers the three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at $St=0.6$ by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics ($St$-$3St$). Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework indicates potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.

#10807. VISOR: A Vision-Language Selector for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (210 w)

VISOR: A Vision-Language Selector for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31780v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent time-series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast a distribution over futures, and multimodal time-series (TS) forecasting further exploits other modalities to improve forecasting accuracy. However, existing works have two limitations: 1) TSFMs reduce the predictive distribution to its median or mean, flattening diverse futures into a calm line, and 2) multimodal TS forecasting models incorporate text into the forecaster through TS-language alignment, which is substantially weaker than vision-language alignment. To address these limitations, we propose the VIsion-language SelectOR (VISOR), a multimodal TS forecasting framework that selects one plausible future instead of averaging across candidates, leveraging the alignment capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to select the most suitable candidate based on textual information. VISOR consists of two components: 1) a text-free stochastic predictor that samples diverse candidate futures, and 2) a VLM selector that reads the candidates as a single chart image and selects one based on the text. To avoid overly calm forecasting paths, we train the selector with a shape-aware target that evaluates each candidate based on both point-wise error and path shape. Across three benchmarks covering ten datasets, VISOR achieves the best average ranking in both point and volatility errors compared with TSFMs and multimodal TS forecasting models. Code: https://github.com/seunghan96/VISOR.
